title: wait, notify and guarded blocks
goal: By the end you can write a guarded block with `wait()` in a `while` loop, choose between `notify()` and `notifyAll()`, and build a bounded buffer from scratch.
opening:
Picture a restaurant kitchen. Waiters write each order on a ticket and clip it to a metal bar called the rail. Cooks take the oldest ticket off and cook it. When the rail is empty, a cook waits for the next ticket.

In a program, the rail is a queue (a list where items join at one end and leave from the other). Each waiter and each cook is a thread, a line of work that runs side by side with the others. The lock from the last lesson keeps the rail in order: one thread at a time touches it. But a lock says nothing about waiting. Most first versions either ask the empty rail "anything yet?" millions of times a second, or nap between looks and make each order wait for the nap to end.

Every Java object has a better answer, built into its lock. In this lesson, we'll teach a cook to wait for free, see why a second cook must check again, watch `notify()` stall the kitchen, and build the rail by hand. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Two cook threads wait on an empty rail with `if (rail.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); return rail.removeFirst();`. A waiter thread adds one order and calls `notifyAll()` to wake the waiting cooks. What happens?
options: One cook gets the order and the other goes back to waiting
Both wake; one gets the order and the other throws NoSuchElementException
Neither wakes until a second order arrives
Both cooks get the same order
warmup.why: `notifyAll()` wakes both cooks, and they take the lock back one at a time. The first one takes the order. The second one checked its `if` before it went to sleep, so it calls `removeFirst()` on an empty rail, which throws `NoSuchElementException`. With `while` instead of `if`, it would check again and go back to waiting. The second section runs exactly this program.

sections.h: Waiting for the rail without spinning: the guarded block

aside.title: Why do the Kotlin samples lock on Object()?
aside.body: Kotlin's `Any` stands for `java.lang.Object`, but it doesn't expose `wait()`, `notify()` or `notifyAll()`. To call them, the Kotlin samples in this lesson declare the lock as a `java.lang.Object` itself, `private val lock = Object()`, which earns a compiler warning that the demos silence with `@Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN")`. The usual Kotlin guarded block uses a `ReentrantLock` (a lock object you take and release by calling methods) and a `Condition` (a wait set of its own, attached to that lock) instead: `await()` plays the part of `wait()`, and `signalAll()` the part of `notifyAll()`. Every rule in this lesson holds there unchanged, and lesson 7 of this track covers it.

sections.h: A limit on the rail, and why notify() can stall it
sections.body:
So far only the cooks wait. When a big table orders twelve dishes at once, the cooks fall behind and the waiters keep adding tickets. A rail with no limit grows until the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects, runs out. A real rail holds only so many tickets, so let's give ours a capacity, and make a waiter wait while it's full. At last, a job that suits the name:

```java
while (rail.size() == capacity) lock.wait();   // the waiter's guard: "not full"
```

```kotlin
while (rail.size == capacity) lock.wait()      // the waiter's guard: "not full"
```

A thread that puts work in is called a **producer**, and a thread that takes work out is a **consumer**: our waiters are producers, and our cooks are consumers. Making a fast producer wait for a slow consumer like this is called **backpressure**.

Backpressure also gives the monitor two kinds of waiting threads. Waiters wait for "not full", and cooks wait for "not empty". A monitor has only one wait set, so they all sit on the same bench.

With `notifyAll()`, that's harmless: everyone wakes, and each `while` loop sends back the threads that can't go on. With `notify()`, it isn't. `notify()` wakes one waiting thread, and it doesn't take requests: the JVM picks which one. Here's what that does to a rail with room for one ticket, two waiters and two cooks, where every signal is a `notify()`:

1. The rail is empty, so both cooks wait.
2. Waiter 1 clips a ticket on, and its `notify()` wakes cook 1. Before cook 1 gets the lock, both waiters find the rail full and wait. The bench now holds waiter 1, waiter 2 and cook 2.
3. Cook 1 takes the ticket and calls `notify()`, which happens to wake cook 2, the wrong kind.
4. Cook 2 finds the rail empty and waits again. Cook 1 loops back, finds it empty too, and waits.

Now all four threads wait for a bell nobody is left to ring. No thread holds the lock, so this isn't a deadlock in the textbook sense (the next lesson has those), but the kitchen has stopped just the same. The Try it below gets there fast. One run printed:

```text
using notify()
after 1 s: 8 orders cooked
stalled after 8 orders. Thread states:
  waiter-0: WAITING
  waiter-1: WAITING
  cook-0: WAITING
  cook-1: WAITING
```

Across runs here it stalled after 1 to 8 orders. With both signals switched to `notifyAll()`, the same four threads cooked about 136,000 to 139,000 orders in five seconds and never stalled. Each thread of the wrong kind checks its guard and goes back to waiting, so the right kind always gets a turn. The price is some extra wake-ups, which is cheap next to a stalled kitchen.

**Two kinds of waiting threads on one monitor need notifyAll(). Wake them all, and let each loop decide.**

`notify()` is safe only when every waiting thread waits for the same condition and one change lets at most one of them go on. Our rail with no limit, from the first two sections, qualified: only cooks waited, and one order let one cook go. A rail with a limit never does. For a precise wake-up per kind of waiting thread, give each kind its own `Condition` on a `ReentrantLock`, as lesson 7 of this track shows.

We now have all three pieces: a loop around every `wait()`, a change of state before every signal, and `notifyAll()` when the waiting threads differ. Let's put them together.

sections.h: The bounded buffer, built by hand, and where it stops

compare.title: A guarded buffer in Java and Kotlin

java.title: BoundedBuffer.java

kotlin.title: KotlinGuarded.kt

compare.note: Both versions are the same guarded buffer: the same `while` guard, the same act, and the same signal to every waiting thread. Three things changed in the Kotlin one. `lock.withLock { }` takes and releases a `ReentrantLock` where Java writes `synchronized`. `changed.await()` stands in for `wait()`. And `changed.signalAll()` stands in for `notifyAll()`. The Java version uses the monitor that every object has carried since Java 1.0, and it needs nothing else. The Kotlin version reaches for a `Condition` because Kotlin's `Any` doesn't expose `wait()`. The rules don't change with the tool: `Condition` allows spurious wakeups too, so the `while` stays. What the `Condition` adds is room to grow, because one lock can have several conditions, so producers and consumers could wait separately. Lesson 7 of this track builds exactly that.

worked.title: Wait for a dish, with a deadline

steps.say: A waiter thread waits until the kitchen marks a table's dish as ready. After 30 seconds it gives up, so it can go and tell the table about the delay. Here is the first attempt. Before you read on, find what can go wrong.

It's the `if` bug in a new shape. `wait(30_000)` waits at most 30 seconds, but it can return sooner. A spurious wakeup, or a `notifyAll()` meant for some other condition on the same lock, makes `wait()` return early with `dishReady` still false: after 2 seconds, say, instead of 30. Just moving `wait(30_000)` into a `while` loop is wrong too, because every wake-up would start a fresh 30 seconds. The cure is to set the deadline once and wait only for what's left of it.
The guard loop now checks two things: the condition and the clock. Each pass waits only for the time that's left.

The cook's thread sets the state before it signals, both under the lock, just as the waiters did with the rail. If it runs before anyone waits, nothing is lost: the waiter thread sees `dishReady` and never calls `wait()`. One question before the last step: why does the waiter use `System.nanoTime()` and not `System.currentTimeMillis()`?

`nanoTime()` only ever moves forward, so it measures elapsed time. `currentTimeMillis()` is the wall-clock time, and the computer may move it backwards or forwards when it corrects its clock over the network (with a service called NTP), which would stretch or cut the timeout.

lab.title: Build a bounded buffer with wait and notifyAll
steps: Meet the class. `BoundedBuffer` is this lesson's rail, written for any type of item: `put` adds at the tail and waits while the buffer is full, and `take` removes from the head and waits while it's empty.
Run the tests. All six fail, some only after a few seconds, because the threads that should wait die instead.
Add the fields: a private lock object, an `ArrayDeque` for the items, the capacity. Reject a capacity below 1 in the constructor.
Write `put`: guard with `while (full) lock.wait();`, add at the tail, then `notifyAll()`.
Write `take`: guard with `while (empty) lock.wait();`, remove the head, `notifyAll()`, and return it. Write `size()` under the lock.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more. The test with four producers and four consumers is the one that catches `if` and `notify()` mistakes.
hints: The blocking tests poll `getState()` until it says `WAITING`. A thread that sleeps in a loop shows `TIMED_WAITING` and fails them. Use `wait()` with no timeout.
Call `wait()` and `notifyAll()` on the same object you synchronize on. Calling `wait()` on `this` while holding `lock` throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`.
Don't catch `InterruptedException` inside the buffer. Let it propagate: both methods already declare it.
lab.done_when: All six tests in `BoundedBufferTest` pass, three runs in a row.

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: A guarded block holds the lock, checks a condition, and calls `wait()` until the condition holds. `wait()` gives the monitor back while it waits and takes it again before it returns.
Call `wait()`, `notify()` or `notifyAll()` only while holding that object's monitor, or you get `IllegalMonitorStateException`.
Always `while (!condition) wait();`. Another woken thread may change the state before you get the lock back, and spurious wakeups are allowed.
Change the state, then notify. Wait for a state, never for a bare signal, so an early notification is never lost.
`notify()` wakes one waiting thread of the JVM's choosing. With two kinds of waiting threads on one monitor it can wake the wrong kind and stall everything, so default to `notifyAll()`.

The limit: a monitor has one wait set, so every `notifyAll()` wakes every kind of waiting thread. A `Condition` gives each kind its own (lesson 7), and `ArrayBlockingQueue` does the whole job for you (lesson 9).
closing:
We started with a cook who had nothing to do but wait for the next ticket. We gave it a guarded block, a `while` loop for the second cook and `notifyAll()` for the rail with a limit, and built the rail by hand.

Now search your own code for `.wait(` and `.await(`. Each should sit in a `while` loop that tests a state. An `if`, or a wait with no condition, passes every test until the evening a second cook joins in.

Here, the stalled threads waited with the lock free. Next, we'll go back to the bank, where threads stop while holding locks: two transfers, each holding one account and waiting for the other. How does that happen, and how do you make sure it can't?

options: Nothing, since nobody is waiting
It wakes every thread in the JVM that is waiting on any lock
It throws IllegalMonitorStateException, because the thread doesn't hold lock's monitor
It blocks until some thread waits on lock
quiz.why: `wait`, `notify` and `notifyAll` need the caller to own the object's monitor, so they belong inside `synchronized (lock)`. The JVM checks ownership first, so it doesn't matter that nobody is waiting. "Nothing" would be the right answer for the same call made inside the lock.

quiz.q: A thread wakes up from `lock.wait()` because another thread called `notifyAll()`. When does it run the line after `wait()`?
options: Immediately, in parallel with the notifier
After it gets the monitor back, which is at the earliest when the notifier leaves its synchronized block
Only after every other woken thread has finished
Never: it has to call wait() again
quiz.why: `notifyAll()` doesn't release the lock. The woken thread moves to the entry set and competes for the monitor, and `wait()` returns only once this thread owns it again. Running "immediately" would put two threads inside one monitor, which a monitor never allows. Other woken threads may get the lock first and change the state, which is why the guard checks again.

quiz.q: A rail with room for one ticket has 2 waiters (producers) and 2 cooks (consumers), and both `put` and `take` call `notify()`. Each `wait()` is correctly inside a `while`. What can happen?
options: Nothing bad, because the while loops make it safe
Two cooks take the same ticket
IllegalMonitorStateException
All four threads end up waiting with nobody left to notify them
quiz.why: The `while` loops stop a thread from acting on a false condition. They can't bring back a signal that went to the wrong thread. If a cook's `notify()` wakes the other cook instead of a waiter, that wake-up is wasted, and soon every thread waits. `notifyAll()`, or one `Condition` per kind of waiting thread, fixes it.

quiz.q: A waiter thread calls `lock.wait()` with no condition, "until the dish is ready". The cook thread calls `lock.notifyAll()` when the dish is done. Sometimes the waiter thread waits forever. Why?
options: notifyAll() only wakes threads that started waiting before it was called, so a dish that is ready early is a lost wake-up
wait() without a timeout is not allowed
notifyAll() needs a second call to wake a thread
The waiter thread must call notify() itself
quiz.why: A notification wakes only threads that are already waiting. If the dish is ready first, the signal goes nowhere, and the waiter thread then waits for a signal that already happened. Wait for a state instead: `while (!ready) lock.wait();`, with `ready = true` set before `notifyAll()`. A timeout would only hide the bug.

quiz.q: From A thread's life: a cook thread is parked inside `lock.wait()` and another thread interrupts it. Which is true?
options: wait() returns normally and the interrupt flag stays set
wait() throws InterruptedException at once, without retaking the monitor
Nothing happens until someone calls notify()
wait() retakes the monitor, then throws InterruptedException with the interrupt flag cleared
quiz.why: Like `sleep`, `wait` reacts to an interrupt by throwing `InterruptedException` and clearing the flag. It takes the monitor back first, so your catch or finally block still runs inside the synchronized block. The tempting "at once" answer misses that step: `wait()` never returns or throws without the lock. Restore the flag or let the exception propagate.

flashcards.back: It releases lock's monitor, parks the thread in the wait set (WAITING), and retakes the monitor before it returns.
Another woken thread may change the state before you get the lock back, and spurious wakeups are allowed.

flashcards.front: What happens if you call `wait()` or `notify()` without holding that object's monitor?

flashcards.back: No. The woken threads compete for the monitor after the notifier leaves its synchronized block.

flashcards.front: When is `notify()` safe to use instead of `notifyAll()`?
flashcards.back: Only when every waiting thread waits for the same condition and each change lets at most one of them proceed.
A notify that happens before anyone waits. If the waiting thread has no condition to check, it then waits forever. Fix: wait for a state field, set before notifying.

terms.plain: Waiting by checking a condition over and over in a loop. The thread stays RUNNABLE and keeps a core busy.
Code that waits, under a lock, until a condition holds: `while (!cond) lock.wait();`.
The threads parked in `wait()` on one monitor, waiting to be notified.
The threads waiting to enter a monitor (BLOCKED), including woken threads that must win the lock back.
A return from `wait()` with no notify, interrupt or timeout. Allowed by the spec.
A signal sent before anyone waits for it, so the waiting thread never hears it.
A producer is a thread that puts work into a shared queue; a consumer is a thread that takes work out.
Making a fast producer wait when the consumer can't keep up, instead of buffering without limit.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a friend who is new to threads why a bounded buffer built on one monitor needs `while` loops and `notifyAll()`, and what goes wrong if you use `if` or `notify()` instead.
explain_back.answer: Producers wait for "not full" and consumers wait for "not empty", but with one monitor they share one wait set. When a thread wakes, the state may already have changed again, because other woken threads can get the lock first, and spurious wakeups are allowed. So each waiting thread must check its condition again in a `while` loop. With `if`, a consumer can wake up and remove from an empty buffer. `notify()` wakes one waiting thread of the JVM's choosing, which may be the wrong kind: a consumer waking another consumer wastes the only signal, and soon every thread waits with nobody left to wake them. `notifyAll()` wakes everyone, and the loops send the ones that can't go on back to waiting.

deeper.body:
Timed waits are the same idea with a clock. `wait(millis)` returns when it's notified, interrupted, woken spuriously, or when the time is up, and it doesn't tell you which. That's why the worked example tracks its own deadline with `System.nanoTime()`.

The JVM has had bugs here too. JDK 26 carries a fix titled "Notification can be lost due to interrupt in Object.wait". That's one more reason to use the standard library's queues and synchronizers wherever you can: they are tested far harder than any guarded block you or I will write.

Two notes on observing waits. Java Flight Recorder (JFR), the event recorder built into the JVM, has a `jdk.JavaMonitorWait` event, with the monitor's class, the thread that notified, the timeout and whether it timed out, and JDK 25 added a `jdk.JavaMonitorNotify` event. And on virtual threads (very light threads that the JVM runs on top of a few ordinary carrier threads), `Object.wait()` used to pin, that is, hold on to, the carrier thread. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491) it no longer does in most cases.

Finally, the history. `wait` and `notify` have been in Java since 1.0. `java.util.concurrent` arrived in Java 5 with `Condition`, `BlockingQueue` and friends, built by Doug Lea on a framework called `AbstractQueuedSynchronizer`. Read the source of `ArrayBlockingQueue` and you'll find the same guard, act and signal as in this lesson, written with a `ReentrantLock` and two `Condition`s.
